name: Conscious Capital — Verano Alimentos & the Greenwashing Crisis
description: A four-round, advanced corporate-sustainability simulation set inside Verano Alimentos S.A., a fictional Brazilian food & beverage company (R$3,4 bilhões revenue, 7 plants, ~5.800 employees, ~2.300 smallholder suppliers). On 11 March 2026 a respected NGO accuses Verano of greenwashing and supply-chain labour problems; the hashtag trends, the internal brand-trust index has already fallen from 72 to 61/100, and two retail customers worth 22% of revenue (~R$750M) threaten to delist premium SKUs within 45 days unless they see a credible, verified remediation plan. Playing the new Sustainability Manager with a hard R$28M annual budget (fully addressing everything would cost ~R$52M, forcing prioritisation), you (1) diagnose and prioritise stakeholders through a materiality lens — choosing the most material issue (water/effluent and deforestation-linked sourcing) over the loudest one (retail/consumer PR); (2) allocate the R$28M across candidate CSR initiatives — water-treatment retrofit, smallholder traceability & fair-sourcing, rider-welfare, and a cheap-but-photogenic community programme — concentrating on substantive, value-creating spend rather than thin philanthropy; (3) set the reporting scope, framework (glossy comms vs GRI), assurance level (none / limited / reasonable) and boundary (own operations vs full supply chain), trading credibility against exposure; and (4) integrate the plan into a board-and-retailer pitch, choosing calibrated, evidence-bounded claims over the overclaim that re-triggers the backlash. The math encodes the five Common Errors — salience over materiality, thin photogenic spend, substance without assurance, selective disclosure, and overclaiming in recovery — so each wrong strategy measurably underperforms. Final KPIs track Stakeholder Value Index, Brand Trust recovery (toward 72), Reporting Credibility, and Budget committed against the R$28M cap.

Conscious Capital

An NGO report and a viral post accuse Verano of greenwashing and labour problems in its supply chain. Your "conscious" brand is now the weapon being used against you. Brand trust has fallen from 72 to 61. Two retailers worth 22% of revenue want a verified remediation plan in 45 days — or they delist your premium lines. You have R$28 million and one chance to prove purpose is real, not marketing.

Round 1 — Diagnose & prioritise stakeholders

Your Decisions This Round

Effort to align stakeholders, not rank them by power: 50
Water-treatment retrofit at the two plants — high cost, high materiality
Smallholder traceability & fair-sourcing — addresses deforestation & farmers
Rider-welfare scheme — visible, answers the labour claim
Community / education programme — cheap, popular, photogenic, low materiality
Allocated: R$24M / R$28M cap
Funding everything credibly would cost ~R$52M. Concentrating on material, value-creating initiatives beats spreading the budget thinly across feel-good spend.
Transparency on the weaknesses the NGO already sees: 50
Facilitator (board · retailer · sceptical NGO/journalist)
Your founders embraced "people and planet" early — and now that promise is the very thing being weaponised against you. The CEO told you to make the R$28M count: prove the purpose is real and measurable, not marketing. The loudest pressure is not the most material issue, the budget will not stretch to everything, and real action still reads as spin if you report it with the same unverifiable brochure. Prioritise on materiality, fund what creates real value, disclose credibly, and communicate without overclaiming.
